video.title: Proper Trunk Sequencing will Transform Your Tennis

classification.reason: The coach explains the biomechanics and mental models of trunk-hip rotational sequencing in tennis strokes using figure skating and pro footage.

problem.title_as_question: How can tennis players properly sequence trunk and hip rotation to generate linear power instead of over-rotating?
problem.definition: Tennis players often spin out, over-rotate, or experience slow acceleration because they misjudge trunk-hip sequencing, visualizing a full continuous turn rather than an early trunk command followed by a compact hip power pulse.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of rotational mechanics in tennis groundstrokes
problem.target_player: Tennis players struggling with over-rotation, spinning out, or slow swing acceleration

symptoms.description: The player over-rotates and spins around rather than producing a compact rotational pulse and a linear finish.
The player experiences a slow, awkward acceleration feeling during the swing.
The player rotates the shoulders excessively far forward before the hips fire their power pulse.

causes.statement: Players incorrectly assume the rotational command originates from the legs or the ground rather than understanding the trunk commands rotation while legs act as force multipliers.
When attempting to imitate compact swings, players disrupt the acceleration rhythm by losing the trunk command followed by hip force multiplication.
Players mentally visualize rotating their shoulder line continuously all the way across from preparation to follow-through.
Aiming to rotate all the way through causes the hips to fire their power pulse far too late in the swing cycle, producing spin instead of linear forward drive.

angles.summary: The coach contrasts the figure skater quad jump's continuous spinning objective with the tennis player's need for a compact pulse to generate a linear strike.
The coach addresses the misleading idea that power comes from the ground, clarifying that the trunk commands rotation while the legs act as a force multiplier.
Biomechanically, the upper body initiates rotation while the legs are still loading, and the hips deliver a power pulse in the middle of rotation to multiply speed.
Pro footage of Alcaraz and Federer demonstrates that trunk rotation leads, the hip pulse completes early, and the trunk slows at contact as the arm takes over.
An efficient swing feels like throwing the hip into or behind the ball rather than spinning around the axis.
Players should visualize the forward press slot as the rotational finish line so the hips fire on time and transfer power into a linear finish.

solutions.summary: Say to yourself: 'Rotate with your trunk' to initiate the movement so that the legs naturally recruit as a force multiplier.
Visualize the forward slot position as the end goal of your rotation and focus on throwing the racket into that spot with maximum velocity.
solutions.external_goal: The racket arriving at the forward contact slot

solutions.summary: Cue the feeling of throwing your hip into the ball or behind the ball during the power pulse rather than spinning around.
Visualize reaching peak upper body velocity early in the swing to naturally trigger the brain to fire the hips linearly into the strike.
